ABSTRACT Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) infection can trigger a sustained inflammatory response, often leading to chronic musculoskeletal pain. Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) and their tissue inhibitors (TIMPs) may contribute to the persistence of arthralgia through their involvement in joint tissue remodeling and degradation. This study aimed to evaluate the potential of MMPs and TIMPs as plasma biomarkers of persistent arthralgia in individuals diagnosed with Chikungunya Fever (CHIKF). A prospective cohort study was conducted using plasma samples from 133 CHIKF‐positive individuals recruited during the acute or post‐acute phases. Sociodemographic and clinical data were collected at outpatient visits. At 90 days post‐symptom onset, participants were assessed for persistent arthralgia using a self‐reported Visual Analog Scale (VAS) for joint pain and categorized into two groups: Recovered (VAS 0–3, n = 71) or Persistent Arthralgia (VAS 4–10, n = 62). Plasma levels of MMP‐2, MMP‐9, and TIMP‐2 were quantified using multiplex bead‐based ELISA (LegendPlex), while MMP‐1, MMP‐3, MMP‐14/MT1‐MMP, and TIMP‐1 were measured via sandwich ELISA. Plasma samples from 51 CHIKV‐negative individuals were used as controls. Statistical analyzes were performed using GraphPad Prism v9.0, IBM SPSS Statistics and Stata. Among post‐acute participants, lower MMP‐2 levels were significantly associated with recovery compared to those with persistent arthralgia and to controls. TIMP‐2 levels varied significantly across clinical outcomes, supporting its involvement in CHIKV‐induced pathology. Multivariate analysis identified swollen joints, skin rash, and elevated TIMP‐2 levels during the post‐acute phase as independent predictors of persistent arthralgia in the chronic phase. No significant differences were observed for MMP‐1, MMP‐3, MMP‐9, MMP‐14, or TIMP‐1. These findings suggest a potential role for TIMP‐2 and musculoskeletal manifestations as early indicators of chronic joint symptoms following CHIKV infection. Laboratory of Immunomodulation and New Therapeutic Approaches, Center for Research in Therapeutic Innovation—Suely Galdino (NUPIT‐SG), Center for Biosciences—CB, Federal University of Pernambuco ‐ Recife, PE, 50670‐901, Brazil. 1 Introduction Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) is an arthropod‐borne alphavirus transmitted primarily by Aedes mosquito and responsible for Chikungunya fever (CHIKF), a disease characterized by acute febrile illness with prominent joint involvement [ 1 ]. Although most patients recover from the acute phase within days to weeks, approximately 30%–40% of infected individuals develop chronic musculoskeletal manifestations, most notably persistent arthralgia lasting beyond 90 days after symptom onset [ 2 , 3 , 4 ]. This chronic condition can lead to substantial joint pain, functional disability, absenteeism, and significant reductions in quality of life and mental well‐being [ 5 , 6 ]. The transition from acute to chronic CHIKF remains incompletely understood but appears to involve prolonged or dysregulated inflammatory responses. During the acute phase, CHIKV infection activates innate immune mechanisms—particularly macrophage recruitment and activation—resulting in the release of proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines such as tumor necrosis factor‐alpha (TNF‐α), interleukin‐1β (IL‐1β), and interleukin‐6 (IL‐6) [ 7 , 8 , 9 ]. Persistent elevation of these mediators has been observed in some patients, suggesting a pathogenic link to long‐term joint damage [ 10 ]. One proposed mechanism involves the dysregulation of matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), a family of proteolytic enzymes involved in extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling. In particular, MMP‐1 and MMP‐3 have been implicated in joint tissue degradation and inflammatory arthritis [ 7 , 11 ]. These enzymes are tightly regulated by tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases (TIMPs), primarily TIMP‐1 and TIMP‐2, which serve to preserve ECM integrity and limit joint destruction. Imbalance between MMPs and TIMPs has been well documented in chronic inflammatory joint diseases and may similarly contribute to persistent arthralgia following CHIKV infection [ 12 , 13 ]. Despite these insights, there remains a lack of validated biomarkers for predicting which individuals will progress to chronic CHIKF. While recent studies have highlighted inflammatory signatures that persist into the chronic phase, the precise roles of MMPs and TIMPs in CHIKV‐associated arthralgia have not been systematically investigated [ 14 ]. Therefore, the aim of this study is to investigate plasma levels of MMP‐1, MMP‐2, MMP‐3, MMP‐9, MMP‐14, TIMP‐1, and TIMP‐2 as potential biomarkers associated with the clinical outcome of persistent arthralgia in individuals diagnosed with CHIKF. Identifying such biomarkers could improve prognostic assessment and inform the development of targeted therapeutic strategies.

extracted_data.document_summary: This prospective longitudinal cohort study investigated plasma levels of matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) and their tissue inhibitors (TIMPs) as potential biomarkers for persistent arthralgia in individuals diagnosed with Chikungunya Fever (CHIKF). The study aimed to identify factors and biomarkers associated with the development of chronic musculoskeletal symptoms. Key findings indicate that lower plasma MMP-2 levels are associated with clinical recovery, while elevated TIMP-2 levels during the post-acute phase are independent predictors, increasing the odds of developing persistent arthralgia in the chronic phase.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational study on the natural course and clinical outcomes of Chikungunya Fever (CHIKF) infection.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: No therapeutic intervention was applied. This was a prospective cohort study observing disease progression across acute (1-14 days post-symptom onset, DPSO), post-acute (15-89 DPSO), and chronic (≥90 DPSO) phases. Participants were assessed for persistent arthralgia at 90 days post-symptom onset using a self-reported Visual Analog Scale (VAS) for joint pain, with plasma samples collected during initial enrollment and subsequent follow-ups between 21 and 90 days after recruitment.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: lower in recovered individuals, higher in persistent arthralgia
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly lower levels were observed in CHIK+ subjects compared to controls (p=0.013) and specifically in recovered individuals compared to controls (p=0.0193, p=0.037). Conversely, elevated levels during the post-acute phase were associated with a 2.5-fold higher odds (OR=2.50; 95% CI: 1.24–5.06; p=0.010) of persistent arthralgia in the chronic phase.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinases, crucial for regulating extracellular matrix (ECM) degradation, promoting tissue regeneration, and involved in inflammation and tissue remodeling. It limits joint destruction by regulating MMP activity and stimulates collagen synthesis.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Chikungunya Fever (CHIKF) infection across acute, post-acute, and chronic phases, particularly in predicting persistent arthralgia versus clinical recovery.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Lower levels are associated with recovery from CHIKF, potentially indicating effective tissue repair. Elevated levels during the post-acute phase are an independent predictor of persistent arthralgia, suggesting ongoing pathological tissue remodeling and inflammation. It is a potential early indicator of chronic joint symptoms, though its diagnostic performance as a standalone predictor was limited.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly lower levels were observed in recovered individuals compared to controls (p=0.017) and to those with persistent arthralgia (p=0.027). These lower levels were associated with recovery. While some general comparisons showed no significant differences, specific analyses for recovered versus persistent arthralgia showed a significant decrease.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Matrix metalloproteinase involved in extracellular matrix (ECM) degradation, collagen breakdown, and tissue remodeling. Its overexpression is implicated in fibroblast-like synoviocyte migration and joint damage in chronic inflammatory diseases.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Post-acute phase of Chikungunya Fever (CHIKF) infection, specifically in individuals who recovered from arthralgia compared to controls and individuals with persistent arthralgia.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Lower levels are associated with clinical recovery from CHIKF and a favorable clinical trajectory, potentially indicating reduced pathological tissue remodeling and joint damage. Its specific role in CHIKF pathogenesis requires further elucidation.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: No statistically significant differences were observed between CHIK+ subjects and controls, nor between Control, Recovered, and Persistent Arthralgia groups.
